sentences.text: Langstonia is an extinct genus of crocodylomorph, with the type species designated as Langstonia huilensis.
The holotype dentary fragment is 68% larger than that of the Argentine species Sebecus icaeorhinus and is proportionally thinner with more recurved and laterally compressed teeth.

The premaxilla of the type specimen measures 12.8 cm in length and is described as tall and thin with fine grooves on its outer surface, while known fossil material includes a complete left premaxilla with a preserved tooth and a piece of the left maxilla with two tooth sockets.

Langstonia teeth are zyphodont with very flattened sides, slightly curved backs, serrated edges containing 5-6 denticles per millimeter, and no grooves on their surface, implying a skull that was high and laterally flattened unlike the horizontally flattened skulls of modern crocodiles.

A single tooth found in the Inuya and Mapuya localities of the Amazon region in Peru is indistinguishable in size and shape from Langstonia huilensis.
The genus Langstonia was established in 2007 by Alfredo Paolillo and Omar Linares.
The name Langstonia honors the paleontologist Wann Langston Jr., and the genus lived during the Middle Miocene in northern South America.
Langstonia lived during the Middle Miocene, specifically the Laventan land-mammal age, between 21 and 17.5 million years ago during the Aquitanian to Burdigalian stages.

Fossils of Langstonia have been found in the Monkey Beds of the Villavieja Formation in Colombia, and the specimens were formally described in 1965 by Wann Langston, Jr., who published a monograph on fossil crocodilians from Colombia.

The first fossils were discovered in the Huila province of Colombia by geologist José Royo y Gómez, and additional fragments were recovered in 1976 at the Monkey Pod locality by Dr. Ernest Lundelius Jr.

Langstonia possessed elongated limbs and a stiff back, adaptations ideal for running and supporting its weight on land, and the type fossil of Langstonia is larger than Sebecus icaeorhinus and has flatter jaws and teeth, implying a skull that was high and laterally flattened unlike the horizontally flattened skulls of modern crocodiles.

Researcher Busbey suggested that Langstonia's high skull implied a hunting strategy of producing quick cuts to weaken prey through bleeding, similar to Komodo dragons, rather than holding pressure indefinitely, and Langstonia was likely a terrestrial apex predator in its ecosystem, outcompeting large mammalian predators and predatory birds of the time.

Fossil evidence indicates Langstonia lived in a warm, humid climate with heavy rainfall and short droughts (3-4 months), inhabiting watersheds, forests, and open grasslands, and Langstonia lived in a warm, humid environment with river basins, forests, and open grasslands where it hunted various megafauna.

Langstonia is classified within Sebecosuchia, a lineage of ziphodont terrestrial crocodylomorphs from the southern continent of Gondwana, and Langstonia is classified as part of Sebecosuchia, a lineage of terrestrial ziphodont crocodylomorphs from the ancient southern continent of Gondwana.

Phylogenetic analysis places Langstonia in a clade within Sebecidae next to Sebecus icaeorhinus and Zulmasuchus, distinct from Barinasuchus and Bretesuchus, and some authors, including Pol (2011, 2012) and Cavalho et al. (2010), still maintain both species within the genus Sebecus.
